digifact-gsz3.content: The DigiByte blockchain launched in 2014. Thanks to its 15 second block time, it is the longest UTXO blockchain in existence with over $blocks_tot_mil million blocks. Bitcoin will take until the 22nd century to reach that many blocks.

digifact-7ttm.content: DigiByte has upgraded the network a number of times to include "Improvement milestones". These hard forks were not contentious splits that generated additional coins, but rather a "reorientation of the ship" that the DigiByte community was onboard with.

digifact-fbnc.content: The DigiByte blockchain was fairly launched in 2014, long before the 2017 Initial Coin Offering (ICO) craze of whitepaper projects. DigiByte began with a fully working blockchain that has been improved upon consistently ever since.

digifact-3tsn.content: When DigiByte launched in 2014, a tiny DigiByte pre-mine (0.5%) was given away to community members within the first 30 days, and the details can be seen on BitcoinTalk. This was done to incentivize people to download and run a full node helping to distribute the blockchain. None of the pre-mine was retained by the founder or developers.

digifact-zbrf.content: There is no founders reward with the DigiByte blockchain. The reward for mining each block only ever goes to whoever mined it. No part of it goes to anyone else.

digifact-c6ds.content: The DigiByte founder and developers have either purchased their DGB coins on an exchange at market rates, or mined them, just like everybody else. There was no ICO (Initial Coin Offering) for the DigiByte blockchain. Every coin has been fairly mined since the genesis block.

digifact-g4d8.content: Transaction fees on the DigiByte blockchain are typically incredibly low. In Block 7658349, a user sent 342,000,000 DGB (worth 6 million USD at the time) from the inputs of over 200 different addresses. It cost 1/10th of a cent (USD) in fees and took only a minute or two to confirm.

digifact-2fm8.content: DigiByte pioneered the DigiShield difficulty adjustment. It's used in Dogecoin, Ubiq, ZCash, Monacoin and parts of the code are even used in Ethereum.
digifact-2fm8.link_social: What is DigiShield (a.k.a MultiShield)? Learn more: https://josiah-digibyte.medium.com/lets-talk-about-multialgo-multishield-45e6a375a7a
digifact-2fm8.link_html: What is DigiShield (a.k.a MultiShield)? Learn more here.
digifact-2fm8.link_md: What is DigiShield (a.k.a MultiShield)? Learn more [here](https://josiah-digibyte.medium.com/lets-talk-about-multialgo-multishield-45e6a375a7a).

digifact-8b5z.content: DigiByte was the first non-Bitcoin blockchain to fix the major inflation bug in 2018. Rapid response from our rock-star developers!

digifact-9kh4.content: The DigiByte 'Genesis Block' contained the following headline: 'USA Today: 10/Jan/2014, Target: Data stolen from up to 110M customers.' This forever cemented DigiByte's focus on cybersecurity.

digifact-g2h8.content: DigiByte was the first coin to upgrade from a single mining algorithm to MultiAlgo, for the additional security provided by having 5x algorithms. This upgrade occurred in late 2014 as the 'MultiAlgo' network upgrade.

digifact-q5s8.content: Initially, DigiByte only used the Scrypt algorithm for mining. In September 2014, the network upgraded to MultiAlgo, utilizing Scrypt, SHA256, Skein, Qubit & Myriad-Groestl. This massively improved decentralization by enabling a broader variety of mining hardware to be used.

digifact-9qrc.content: In 2019, DigiByte upgraded the network, replacing the Myriad-Groestl algorithm with Odocrypt, an algorithm designed to be ASIC-resistant by targeting mining with FPGA hardware. However, with most ASIC-resistant algorithms, if the financial incentives are there, eventually ASICs will be developed for these algorithms, as is the case with Odocrypt.

digifact-rtw2.content: In 2018, the DigiByte community raised enough funds to supply Venezuelan refugees crossing the border with over a thousand bottles of water, feed 160 orphaned children for a month, provide essential maintenance for a hospital, refurbish an Adicora school kitchen, and host several free community lunches for hundreds of people.

digifact-z6qb.content: DigiByte is not an ICO or a token launched on another network, but rather a pure blockchain project with its own consensus rules like Bitcoin or Litecoin.

digifact-5txj.content: For general DigiByte support, a good place to start is with the community support tool available

digifact-2dtn.content: DigiByte can be used to store tiny amounts (80-bytes) of data along with a transaction known as OP_RETURN. This is useful for document hashes for notarization/validation, dApps, scripting, and more.

digifact-xs6z.content: You can look up any transaction on the DigiByte Blockchain by inputting a transaction ID, DigiByte address, or block number into a 'Blockchain Explorer'.
digifact-xs6z.link_social: The community maintains one such explorer you can use at: https://digiexplorer.info
digifact-xs6z.link_html: The community maintains one such explorer you can use here
digifact-xs6z.link_md: The community maintains one such explorer you can use [here](https://digiexplorer.info/)

digifact-cmq8.content: The name 'DigiByte' was originally chosen as it signifies a 'Digital Byte' of data. This is because blockchain technology such as DigiByte can be used for so much more than as a 'coin' such as silver or gold. DigiByte is incredibly multi-purpose.

digifact-rwvq.content: A copy of the DigiByte blockchain open source code v7.17.3 is lying in cold storage 250 meters deep in the permafrost of an Arctic mountain! Thanks to the GitHub Arctic Code Vault program!

digifact-nzcz.content: DigiByte is available on many exchanges around the world, including many different fiat pairings with local currencies, making it easy to buy DigiByte.

digifact-qmjp.content: DigiByte was founded by Jared Tate in 2013 and the Genesis block was mined on 10th January 2014. While Jared remains an active member of the DigiByte community, and is one of the Core developers, he does not dictate the direction of the project. DigiByte has no boss - it is entirely run and managed by a global community of dedicated volunteers.

digifact-gh7t.content: DigiByte can do smart contracts thanks to its 'script' language. You can run a whole lot of powerful tools on top of DigiByte to power a dApp.

digifact-2ppj.content: The official DigiByte Core wallet is available for Windows, macOS and Linux, as well as low-powered single-board computers like the Raspberry Pi. DigiByte is also supported by many third-party wallets on mobile and desktop, and by hardware wallets such as Ledger. Be advised that not all wallets support Digi-ID, DigiAssets or DigiDollar.

digifact-s4gj.content: Digi-ID by DigiByte is one of the simplest yet most secure authentication methods in the world. Even Google warns against using their own time-based 2FA codes or SMS-2FA, but Digi-ID overcomes all the shortcomings. Digi-ID is open source, free, ad-free (forever), private & secure.

digifact-3zcz.content: The development of DigiByte is done by a worldwide team of volunteers, who all donate their time out of a passion for the project. There is no central company employing and paying people, it's all given freely by our incredible developers and supporting community.

digifact-k8qp.content: The last DigiByte will be mined by the year 2035. There is less than half of all remaining DGB waiting to be mined by anybody in the world. These are not 'owned' by anybody, unlike an ICO and will be newly 'minted'.

digifact-v3nn.content: DigiByte can be used for Atomic Swaps with other blockchains safely and securely since the implementation of SegWit in early 2017. There is no need for a second layer network to perform this and it can instead be done directly.

digifact-xtxt.content: When all DigiByte have been mined, the network will continue to function with the miners mining / securing the network as they do at present. They will only get the transaction fees from sending DGB.

digifact-7n3j.content: If you ever have issues with getting your DigiByte out of a wallet, you can sweep the funds to a new wallet using the DigiSweep tool created by DigiByte community member Matthew Cornelisse. It's easy to use & open-source.

digifact-cbwt.content: When DigiByte launched, there was a countdown to the release of the code, and to the first block being mined. This was one of the things done to encourage a "fair" distribution, right from the very beginning in 2014.

digifact-9t6n.content: DigiByte was originally based on a fork of the Litecoin code-base (Though, a 100% independent blockchain with unique Genesis Block). DigiByte has since maintained closer features with Bitcoin, while also significantly innovating and surpassing it!

digifact-5fq3.content: Anyone can build second-layer networks on top of the DigiByte Blockchain, such as DigiAssets, Lightning Networks, ICOs, Tokens, assets and more.

digifact-fdtw.content: There's a mind-boggling number of possible DigiByte addresses. 1,461,501,637,330,902,918,203,684,832,716,283,019,655,932,542,976 (2¹⁶⁰). This is a quindecillion. It's so big you could randomly generate trillions of addresses a second and never generate the same one twice.

digifact-dk5q.content: You can accept DigiByte in retail scenarios just by entering the desired amount into your wallet. The QR code will automatically include your address and the amount when the sender scans it. Super simple, straight from your wallet.

digifact-vpb3.content: The DigiByte Core wallet connects to a variety of peers, not just the 'closest' or 'fastest'. It finds connections from all over the world, to ensure you get a broad consensus on the DigiByte blockchain and protects you against sybil attacks.

digifact-bd3t.content: DigiByte implemented the DigiSpeed protocol in 2015. This allowed DigiByte to decrease from 30 second to 15 second block timings. Lightning fast!

digifact-7m9n.content: Did you know that DigiByte is permissionless? This means there is no individual or company to ask if you can build a dApp on top of it, use it, send it, receive it, accept it for your business, advertise it, promote it. You simply "can"!

digifact-2k8q.content: The DigiAsset Explorer, created by DigiByte community member Renzo Diaz, makes it easy to lookup information about DigiAsset transactions.

digifact-3dz3.content: DigiBytes MultiAlgo means 5x algorithms all continuously compete for every single block. Others such as X16R are very different, instead rotating through each sub-algorithm with all miners swapping and using that same. As such, X16R is still a "single algorithm" compared with DigiBytes 5x MultiAlgo implementation.

digifact-fk8g.content: The Dandelion privacy protocol was implemented in 2019, to help protect your privacy, by masking the originating IP address.
digifact-fk8g.link_social: To learn more about Dandelion, visit: https://josiah-digibyte.medium.com/digibyte-flowers-with-dandelion-2239b2bbdd46
digifact-fk8g.link_html: Go here to learn more about Dandelion.
digifact-fk8g.link_md: Go [here](https://josiah-digibyte.medium.com/digibyte-flowers-with-dandelion-2239b2bbdd46) to learn more about Dandelion.

digifact-dccw.content: MultiShield is a powerful difficulty adjustment algorithm. It ensures each of DigiBytes 5X algorithms all mine roughly an equal amount of blocks, while maintaining a steady 15 second timing.
digifact-dccw.link_html: What is MultiShield? Learn more here.

digifact-r7k4.content: Because of MultiShield, DigiByte has some of the most accurate and stable block-timings. Where other projects usually wait for 3-4 days to adjust, MultiShield tweaks, adjusts & refines every single block.

digifact-kpfs.content: DigiByte was the first major blockchain project to enable the Dandelion privacy protocol, to protect your IP address. You can opt out of the privacy-protection it offers if you want even faster transactions.
digifact-kpfs.link_social: To learn more about Dandelion, visit: https://josiah-digibyte.medium.com/digibyte-flowers-with-dandelion-2239b2bbdd46
digifact-kpfs.link_html: Go here to learn more about Dandelion.
digifact-kpfs.link_md: Go [here](https://josiah-digibyte.medium.com/digibyte-flowers-with-dandelion-2239b2bbdd46) to learn more about Dandelion

digifact-vjx7.content: DigiByte is all about choice, and what works for you personally. DigiByte is supported by many different wallets, so there's something that will fit everyone's requirements.

digifact-w3p6.content: DigiByte originally had 60 second block timings, however through multiple network upgrades that were improved upon, first to 30, and now to the 15 seconds it is today.

digifact-7mzk.content: DigiByte has had 100% uptime since its launch. While some people restart their computers from time to time, hundreds of others remain online all the time so that even in the event of a major nationwide internet outage, DigiByte would still continue to function.

digifact-zmwg.content: Anybody is able to contribute to the DigiByte code and make improvements. All submissions get reviewed by other developers to ensure no malicious code is accidentally accepted.
digifact-zmwg.link_social: Join the Gitter developer chat here: https://gitter.im/DigiByte-Core/protocol
digifact-zmwg.link_html: Join the Gitter developer chat here.

digifact-4km6.content: Nobody knows exactly how many "nodes" there are on the DigiByte network, because there is no central point that all computers check in with. This ensures your privacy when you download the wallet software.

digifact-6j3k.content: DigiByte has never had a contentious hard fork despite ongoing major code changes. Mining is so decentralized that when the myriad-groestl algorithm was replaced with odocrypt, MG mining pools installed the upgrade even when it meant they would no longer be able to mine.

digifact-j6cb.content: DigiByte mining is some of the most distributed in the industry. When a 7-day period in September 2019 was compared against Bitcoin and Litecoin, DigiByte had over 10X the number of unique miners. This grew to over 20X the unique miners when looking at a 3-month period.

digifact-2jxq.content: If the biggest 5x pools from Bitcoin were to collude, they could control the Bitcoin, Bitcoin Cash, and Bitcoin SV networks permanently until others grew to have more hash-power than them. Those same pools would not be a threat to DigiByte thanks to DigiBytes MultiAlgo and MultiShield aspects.

digifact-tj8g.content: Every month, the DigiByte that miners get as a block-reward is decreased by 1%. This gives DigiByte a very smooth supply-curve for new DigiByte, rather than a "halving" event every few years.

digifact-9zx9.content: Transactions on the DigiByte network are public, but pseudo-anonymous. You can see them on a Blockchain explorer, however there is nothing inherently that can link a new transaction / address to an end-user. There are no usernames, email addresses etc required to use the DigiByte network.

digifact-j4ng.content: DigiByte addresses can be re-used, but it's completely optional. The best practice is for a wallet to give you a new address each time after your previous address has received a transaction.

digifact-8wqz.content: The source code for the DigiByte blockchain is completely open-source, anybody can see it, inspect it, and review it.
digifact-8wqz.link_social: Find it on GitHub here: https://github.com/DigiByte-Core/DigiByte

digifact-skpt.content: DigiByte blocks have an expected 15 second time, which means every single day there are 5,760 new blocks added to the DigiByte blockchain.

digifact-gfgk.content: A single DigiByte can be divided up to 8 decimal places. That's 1/100,000,000 of a DigiByte. This is known as a Digit or DIT for short. (e.g. 1000 DITS)

digifact-d4rg.content: Each of the 5x algorithms that DigiByte uses to secure the network and mine new blocks has an equal 20% chance to find every single block. There is no priority given to one or another.

digifact-5qj7.content: DigiByte has four types of address, each starting with a different prefix. Modern addresses start with "dgb1": "dgb1q" for SegWit (Bech32) addresses and "dgb1p" for Taproot addresses. Older addresses start with the letter "S" (wrapped SegWit) or "D" (Legacy). While support for these will remain, they are gradually being phased out.

digifact-sw8j.content: DigiByte addresses starting with "dgb1" (known as Bech32 format) have multiple advantages, such as error correction in the event they were incorrectly written-down, as well as being much easier for both humans and computers to recognize that they are DigiByte-specific addresses.

digifact-qmm2.content: For a protocol upgrade to take place, over 70% of the network must agree and be in consensus that the upgrade will take place. This occurs by "signaling" support for it when blocks are mined, over the course of a 1-week period.

digifact-v3cx.content: There is a maximum of 21 billion DigiByte that will ever exist. This was intentionally chosen as a 1000:1 ratio compared to Bitcoins 21 million. No more can ever be created.

digifact-3pp9.content: DigiByte is available on Crypto ATMs around the world! This is a great way for people new to cryptocurrency to get involved through a more "traditional" method of currency exchange.

digifact-dzrh.content: DigiByte can be used to verify and validate documents, music, media, identity and more! Although DigiByte excels as a means of exchanging value, it is not limited to just being a currency.

digifact-ttjt.content: You can use multiple wallets! DigiByte is not just limited to a single piece of software, and the community is encouraged to find an app that works best for them, so try one, try a few, and keep using the ones you like the most.

digifact-bpfn.content: DigiByte cannot ever have a centralized "burning" of the maximum supply as other ICO's or centrally controlled tokens can. Because DigiByte is a fully decentralized project, it's impossible to issue a large-scale "burning" of unused DigiByte. At most, you could only ever destroy your own if you willingly transferred them in to the void.

digifact-db2z.content: Transactions on the DigiByte blockchain cannot be undone, by anybody. Once a transaction has been made, it is permanent. Did you accidentally send 50 DigiByte instead of 5 DigiByte? You'll need to ask the recipient to return the surplus, as there is no "Undo" function, and no central banking authority who can roll back transactions.

digifact-tbts.content: Do you want to start a DigiByte podcast, or meet-up? Go for it! There is nobody to ask for permission, part of DigiByte being a "permissionless" project. It is implied that you can, so go right ahead and do it.

digifact-cchd.content: If you have ever had the misfortune to accidentally send your DigiByte to a Dogecoin address, your coins may not be lost. DigiSweep by DigiByte community member Matthew Cornelisse (@mctrivia) may be able to help you recover them.

digifact-bjqp.content: The DigiByte subreddit located at r/DigiByte is a great place to stay updated about all the news and developments in the DigiByte community.

digifact-s9q5.content: The DigiByte Discord server is where you will find the most active members of the DigiByte community, and is a great way to connect with all the people working on DigiByte behind the scenes.

digifact-np2q.content: DigiNode Tools is a software suite that makes it easy to set up and manage a DigiByte node on a low-power device like a Raspberry Pi, or on a Debian or Ubuntu system. Setup is menu-driven, with detailed step-by-step instructions, and you can even set up a Dual Node to run both a mainnet and a testnet node on the same device.

digifact-wr7h.content: These DigiFacts are written by the DigiByte community, for the DigiByte community. Anyone can help - by suggesting new DigiFacts, fixing mistakes, or improving the translations.
digifact-wr7h.link_social: Go here to learn how you can help: https://github.com/DigiNode-Tools/digibyte-digifacts
digifact-wr7h.link_html: Go here to learn how you can help.
digifact-wr7h.link_md: Go [here](https://github.com/DigiNode-Tools/digibyte-digifacts) to learn how you can help.

digifact-v5ds.content: You can display these DigiFacts on a Tidbyt, or any other LED pixel display running Tronbyt. The free DigiFacts app shows the DigiFact of the day or a random one, in eight languages, and DigiFacts with a link end with a QR code you can scan with your phone.

digifact-nqzd.content: You can keep an eye on DigiByte's price with the DigiByte Price app for Tronbyt. It shows the current price of DGB in up to four currencies, including Satoshis, on a Tidbyt or any other LED pixel display running Tronbyt, and updates every 10 minutes.

digifact-n8xm.content: A DigiByte Seeder is a lightweight DNS server run by a few trusted volunteers from the DigiByte community. It continuously crawls the DigiByte network looking for nodes and maintains a list of the IP addresses and ports of the most reliable ones. DigiByte Nodes joining the network use the DigiByte Seeders to find other nodes to connect to.

digifact-nhjh.content: The website "DigiByte Facts" is a fantastic learning resource created by a member of the DigiByte community. It offers many of these DigiFacts as shareable images, along with quizzes and other resources to help you learn more about DigiByte.

digifact-cz5m.content: For developers, DigiByte JS is a pure and powerful Javascript DigiByte library forked from Bitpay's Bitcore Lib library.

digifact-h4n2.content: DigiAssets are a secure, scalable second-layer built on top of the DigiByte Blockchain that allows for the decentralized issuance of digital assets (NFTs), tokens, smart contracts, digital identity and more.

digifact-t2gb.content: DigiAsset Core is the most recent implementation of the DigiAsset protocol. Spearheaded by community member Matthew Cornelisse, it runs alongside a DigiByte Core node and helps decentralize DigiAssets and their metadata. DigiAsset Core is not part of DigiByte Core - it is an independent but complementary community-driven project.

digifact-4cg4.content: The DigiByte Awareness Team (DGBAT) regularly runs community votes, where you vote with DGB. Each project on the ballot has its own DigiByte address, and how much is sent to it is the weight of the vote. When a vote closes, the whole pot is shared between the projects in those proportions, all visible on the DigiByte blockchain.

digifact-zfg8.content: DigiHash is a community mining pool for DigiByte, supporting all five of DigiByte's mining algorithms. Ten percent of the pool fee goes back into the community fund for DigiByte development.

digifact-q3r6.content: DigiByte Open Nodes is a live map of the DigiByte network. It shows which nodes can be reached, which version of DigiByte Core each one runs, where in the world they are and how reliable they've been, and it has guides to help you add your own node.

digifact-k9j6.content: DigiDollar is DigiByte's own stablecoin, designed to keep a steady value of one US dollar. It went live on the DigiByte network on 17 July 2026, at block 23,869,440. It has no issuer, no custodian and no admin key: every DigiDollar is backed by DGB locked on the DigiByte blockchain.

digifact-5gxq.content: To create DigiDollars, you lock DGB in a time-locked vault on the DigiByte blockchain, secured by your own keys. Locks last from 1 hour to 10 years, and shorter locks need more DGB, from 10 times the DigiDollar value down to twice it. When the lock ends, you return the DigiDollars to unlock your DGB.
digifact-5gxq.link_social: Read the DigiDollar white paper here: https://www.digibyte.org/docs/DigiDollar_whitepaper.pdf
digifact-5gxq.link_html: Read the DigiDollar white paper here.

digifact-k5kv.content: DigiDollar gets the price of DGB from a network of 35 independent price oracles. Each takes the median DGB/US dollar price from at least three exchanges, and at least 7 oracles must agree and sign the price together before it can be used, so no single oracle can set it.

digifact-qhrt.content: DigiDollar is only created inside the official DigiByte Core wallet, and creating it never requires sending your DGB to anyone. Be wary of any website, bot or app that asks you to send DGB to "mint DigiDollar", or asks for your seed phrase or private keys.

digifact-zgg5.content: Because DigiDollar's DGB collateral is time-locked, it can never be force-sold if the price of DGB falls. Instead, DigiDollar protects itself automatically: when the system is under stress, creating new DigiDollars needs more DGB, and in an emergency more DigiDollars are needed to unlock DGB.

digifact-njvr.content: DigiByte supports Taproot, the upgrade that brought Schnorr signatures and more private, efficient smart contracts to Bitcoin. It arrived with DigiByte Core v8.26, built on Bitcoin Core 26, and has been active since block 21,168,000.

digifact-f3j7.content: A blockchain is a shared record of transactions, kept by thousands of computers around the world instead of one company. New transactions are grouped into blocks, and each block is linked to the one before it, so changing an old record would mean redoing everything that came after it.

digifact-c2fp.content: A DigiByte "node" is a computer that keeps its own copy of the DigiByte blockchain and checks every transaction and block against the rules for itself. Nobody has to trust anyone else: each node verifies everything independently.

digifact-mbc8.content: Mining is how new blocks are added to DigiByte. Miners compete to solve a difficult puzzle, and whoever solves it first adds the next block and earns the block reward. The work this takes is what makes rewriting DigiByte's history so expensive - this is called "proof of work".

digifact-cdmk.content: Your DigiByte address is like an email address: you can share it freely so people can send you DGB. Your private key is like the password - whoever has it controls the DGB, so it should never be shared with anyone.

digifact-wbhn.content: Most wallets back up your private keys as a "seed phrase" of 12 or 24 words. Anyone with those words can take your DGB, so write them down and keep them somewhere safe and offline. No real wallet, exchange or support team will ever ask you for them.

digifact-mq7d.content: "Not your keys, not your coins": if you keep DGB on an exchange, the exchange holds the keys and you are trusting it with your coins. In your own wallet, you are the only one in control.

digifact-gvc6.content: Each new block added after your transaction is one more "confirmation", making it ever harder to reverse. With DigiByte's 15 second blocks, six confirmations take about a minute and a half - on Bitcoin, the same takes about an hour.

digifact-jsmz.content: Transaction fees on DigiByte depend on the size of the transaction in bytes, not on how much DGB you send. Sending 1 DGB or 1 million DGB in a simple transaction costs the same.

digifact-s3kn.content: DigiByte keeps track of coins like banknotes, in a design called "UTXO" (unspent transaction outputs). When you pay, your wallet spends whole "notes" and sends the change back to a new address of yours - which is why a wallet sometimes shows addresses you didn't create yourself.

digifact-bfwh.content: DigiByte also runs a "testnet" - a separate, public DigiByte network where the coins have no value - so developers can try out new ideas without risking real DGB.

digifact-dq7n.content: One of DigiByte's five mining algorithms, Odocrypt, changes itself every 10 days. This makes it very hard to build dedicated mining chips (ASICs) for it, so it is mined with reprogrammable chips called FPGAs.

digifact-cbqx.content: DigiByte activated SegWit in April 2017, ahead of both Litecoin and Bitcoin. SegWit fixed a long-standing weakness called transaction malleability, and made room for upgrades like the Lightning Network and Taproot.

digifact-smzd.content: You can run a full DigiByte node - one that checks every rule for itself - using only a few gigabytes of storage instead of the whole blockchain (about 40 GB). This is called a "pruned" node: it keeps the recent blocks it needs and discards older ones.

digifact-2k5s.content: DigiByte Core can connect to the DigiByte network over Tor, hiding your node's IP address from the other nodes it talks to.

digifact-8brz.content: Because DigiByte has no company behind it, nobody can freeze your DGB, block a payment or close your account. The network follows the same rules for everyone.

digifact-pk8d.content: Anyone can propose an improvement to DigiByte through a DigiByte Improvement Proposal (DIP), which the community and developers discuss in the open.

digifact-pt5c.content: DGB has no company, government or bank behind it. Its value comes entirely from the people who choose to use it, hold it, mine it and build on it.

digifact-jvsk.content: New DGB only ever comes into existence as block rewards for the miners who secure the network. There are no pre-sales, no company treasury, and no way to create extra coins.

digifact-6n7w.content: The maximum of 21 billion DGB is set in DigiByte's consensus rules, which every node checks. Changing it would need the whole network to agree, so no individual or group can quietly create more.

digifact-z5vw.content: Miners earn the block reward plus transaction fees for securing DigiByte. As the block reward shrinks each month, transaction fees will gradually become a bigger part of what pays for the network's security.

digifact-spwn.content: DGB that is locked to create DigiDollars can't be spent until its lock ends - anything from 1 hour to 10 years later.

digifact-zq9t.content: Writing about DigiByte? The official DigiByte media kit has logos, colours and key facts.

digifact-j2nw.content: The official DigiByte logos - including those for Digi-ID, DigiAssets and DigiDollar - are free for anyone to use, under the MIT licence.

digifact-9tqw.content: Want to accept DGB in your business or app, or list it on an exchange? The official DigiByte integration guide explains how.

digifact-3bcd.content: For an in-depth look at how DigiByte works - its architecture, security and ecosystem - the official DigiByte technical guide covers it all.

digifact-p5p8.content: Running your own DigiByte node is one of the best ways to support the network. Every node independently checks the rules and helps new nodes join.

digifact-2z3t.content: DigiDollar has its own official logos, so wallets, exchanges and apps that support it can show it consistently.

digifact-vxhg.content: DigiByte Blockchain Stats shows live statistics about the DigiByte network, including blocks, the hashrate of each mining algorithm, the supply of DGB and DigiDollar.

digifact-t8sq.content: A mining algorithm is the puzzle miners solve to add a block. Miners run the block's data through a hash function again and again, changing a number each time, until the result is below a target. The only way to find one is trial and error - so it takes real work - but anyone can check the answer instantly.

digifact-ck2q.content: Each mining algorithm is a different kind of puzzle, so a machine built for one can't mine another. That's why DigiByte's five algorithms let five different kinds of mining hardware help secure the same network.

digifact-zbnq.content: Today, DigiByte's five mining algorithms are SHA256, Scrypt, Skein, Qubit and Odocrypt. Each one can find the next block, so no single type of mining hardware can dominate the network.

digifact-v2r3.content: SHA256 is one of DigiByte's five mining algorithms. It's the same algorithm Bitcoin uses, so the same mining machines that mine Bitcoin can also help secure DigiByte.

digifact-b3hn.content: Scrypt was DigiByte's only mining algorithm when it launched in 2014, and it is still one of its five today. Litecoin and Dogecoin use it too, so their mining machines can mine DigiByte as well.

digifact-nfsn.content: Skein, one of DigiByte's five mining algorithms, is built on the Skein hash function - a finalist in the competition to choose the SHA-3 standard, designed by a team including cryptographer Bruce Schneier. DigiByte runs it together with SHA256.

digifact-3grm.content: Qubit, one of DigiByte's five mining algorithms, chains five different hash functions together: Luffa, CubeHash, SHAvite-3, SIMD and ECHO. Each one is applied in turn to the result of the one before.

digifact-zgsv.content: Odocrypt, the newest of DigiByte's five mining algorithms, was added in July 2019. It replaced Myriad-Groestl, and was designed by DigiByte developers to be mined with reprogrammable FPGA chips rather than dedicated ASICs.

digifact-3r3z.content: Myriad-Groestl was one of DigiByte's five mining algorithms from 2014 until 2019, when it was replaced by Odocrypt. It combined the Groestl hash function - another finalist for the SHA-3 standard - with SHA256. Blocks mined with it are no longer accepted.

digifact-7z7r.content: Regtest ("regression test") is a private DigiByte blockchain that runs only on your own computer. Developers use it to test software: they can create new blocks instantly, whenever they like, with coins that exist nowhere else.

digifact-nfb8.content: DigiByte has more than one network: mainnet (real DGB), testnet (a public test network where coins have no value) and regtest (a private test chain on your own computer). Their addresses look different - dgb1 on mainnet, dgbt1 on testnet and dgbrt1 on regtest - so they can't be mixed up.

digifact-pr8n.content: SegWit, short for Segregated Witness, separates the signatures in a transaction (the "witness") from the rest of its data. This lets each block hold more transactions, and fixed a weakness called transaction malleability.

digifact-mcj6.content: Before SegWit, a transaction's ID could be changed by tweaking its signature, without changing what it does - known as "transaction malleability". This made it unsafe to build on transactions that weren't yet confirmed. SegWit fixed it, making things like atomic swaps and the Lightning Network possible.

digifact-zmm9.content: Because SegWit signature data counts for less when blocks are filled, SegWit transactions - from addresses starting with "dgb1" - usually cost less in fees than ones from older addresses.

digifact-h5tz.content: DigiByte addresses starting with "D" are Legacy addresses, the original type from 2014. They still work, but transactions from them are larger, so they usually cost a little more in fees than modern addresses starting with "dgb1".

digifact-sz9f.content: DigiByte addresses starting with "S" are script addresses. They can hold coins controlled by several keys at once (multisig), or wrap a SegWit address so that older wallets can send to it. Very old script addresses start with "3", and still work.

digifact-qmcr.content: DigiByte addresses starting with "dgb1p" are Taproot addresses. With Taproot, a payment that needs several people's keys, or has complex conditions, can look just like an ordinary payment on the blockchain - more private, and often cheaper.

digifact-wxc6.content: You can send DGB from any type of DigiByte address to any other - from an address starting with "D" to one starting with "dgb1", and back. The type of address only changes how the coins are locked, not the DGB themselves.

digifact-rp4k.content: Every DigiByte address includes a checksum, so a mistyped address is almost always rejected by your wallet before anything is sent.

digifact-wmjg.content: Mining "difficulty" is how hard the mining puzzle is. When more miners join, blocks would come too quickly, so the network raises the difficulty; when miners leave, it lowers it. This keeps a new DigiByte block coming every 15 seconds on average.

digifact-vpv2.content: Bitcoin adjusts its mining difficulty once every 2,016 blocks - about every two weeks - so if many miners leave suddenly, blocks can slow down for days. DigiByte adjusts after every single block, so it recovers within minutes.

digifact-9fh4.content: Each of DigiByte's five mining algorithms has its own difficulty. If one algorithm starts finding blocks too often, its difficulty goes up, and if it finds too few, it goes down. This is MultiShield, and it keeps each algorithm finding about a fifth of the blocks.

digifact-gwp8.content: DigiShield was created in 2014 to protect DigiByte from "multipools" - large groups of miners that jumped onto a blockchain while mining it was easy, then left once the difficulty rose, leaving blocks stuck. By adjusting quickly in both directions, DigiShield made this far less profitable.

digifact-ptd7.content: An ASIC (application-specific integrated circuit) is a chip built to do just one job. A mining ASIC can only run one mining algorithm, but it does so far faster and more efficiently than any computer - which is why DigiByte's SHA256 and Scrypt algorithms are mined mostly with ASICs.

digifact-rwc2.content: An FPGA (field-programmable gate array) is a chip whose circuits can be rewired with new instructions after it has been made. That's what suits it to DigiByte's Odocrypt algorithm: when Odocrypt changes every 10 days, an FPGA can simply be reprogrammed - something a fixed ASIC can't do.

digifact-m7m5.content: Cryptocurrency mining began on ordinary computer processors (CPUs), then moved to graphics cards (GPUs), which can run many calculations at once. Next came FPGAs, and then ASICs - each step faster and more efficient, but more specialised. DigiByte's five algorithms were chosen to give a range of mining hardware a part in securing the network.
